---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:interval}
Let $G_1,\ldots,G_t$ be finite groups, where $t\geqslant 1$, and put
\[
 \mathcal{W}=\mathsf{V}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(G_1)^0,\ldots,\mathcal{P}(G_t)^0\bigr).
\]
Let $H$ be a finite group with $|H|\geqslant 3$. Then every ai-semiring variety $\mathcal{V}$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maininterval}
 \mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H))\subseteq\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{W}
\end{equation}
has infinite axiomatic rank and is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:zerointerval}
Let $G$ be a finite group with $|G|\geqslant 3$. Then every variety in
\[
 [\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(G)),\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(G)^0)]
\]
has infinite axiomatic rank and is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:classification}
Let $G$ be a finite group. Then $\mathcal{P}(G)^0$ is finitely based if and only if $|G|\leqslant 2$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:reduction}
Every finite set $\Sigma$ of ai-semiring identities is equivalent to a finite set $\mathcal{E}$ of inequalities
\[
 \mathbf{q}\preceq\mathbf{u},
\]
where $\mathbf{q}$ is a word and $\mathbf{u}$ is a finite nonempty sum of words.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
For an identity $\mathbf{u}_1+\cdots+\mathbf{u}_a\approx\mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+\mathbf{v}_b$ with word summands, take the inequalities
\[
 \mathbf{u}_i\preceq\mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+\mathbf{v}_b\quad(1\leqslant i\leqslant a),
 \qquad
 \mathbf{v}_j\preceq\mathbf{u}_1+\cdots+\mathbf{u}_a\quad(1\leqslant j\leqslant b).
\]
The two families express the two directions of the original equality in the additive order. Taking their union over $\Sigma$ proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:zeroidentity}
Let $S$ be an ai-semiring, let $\mathbf{q}$ be a word, and let $\mathbf{u}$ be a term. Then
\[
 S^0\models\mathbf{q}\preceq\mathbf{u}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})\ne\varnothing
 \ \text{ and }\ S\models\mathbf{q}\preceq D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u}).
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Assign the new zero to all variables outside $c(\mathbf{q})$ and assign elements of $S$ to those in $c(\mathbf{q})$. The surviving upper summands are exactly those in $D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})$. The value of $\mathbf{q}$ belongs to $S$, so at least one upper summand survives, proving necessity.

Conversely, consider an assignment into $S^0$. If a variable of $\mathbf{q}$ is assigned zero, the lower word evaluates to zero and the inequality holds. Otherwise all variables of $D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})$ receive elements of $S$, and the assumed inequality gives
\[
 \mathbf{q}\leqslant D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})\leqslant\mathbf{u}
\]
under this assignment.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:finitevariable}
Let $A$ be a finite ai-semiring and let $k\geqslant 1$. There is a finite subset $\Delta_k\subseteq\operatorname{Id}_k(A)$ from which every member of $\operatorname{Id}_k(A)$ follows.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $F_k$ be the finite set of $k$-ary term functions of $A$. For each $f\in F_k$, choose a representative term $\mathbf{t}_f$ over $x_1,\ldots,x_k$. Let $p_i$ be the $i$th projection. Include in $\Delta_k$ the identities
\[
 x_i\approx\mathbf{t}_{p_i},\qquad
 \mathbf{t}_f+\mathbf{t}_g\approx\mathbf{t}_{f+g},\qquad
 \mathbf{t}_f\mathbf{t}_g\approx\mathbf{t}_{fg}
 \quad(1\leqslant i\leqslant k,\ f,g\in F_k),
\]
where operations on term functions are pointwise. These identities hold in $A$. Induction on term formation shows that each term is equivalent, modulo $\Delta_k$, to the chosen representative of its term function. Consequently, every identity in $\operatorname{Id}_k(A)$ follows from $\Delta_k$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:local}
Let $\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{W}$ be ai-semiring varieties. Suppose that, for every $k\geqslant 1$, there is an ai-semiring $Q_k$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item every subsemiring of $Q_k$ generated by at most $k$ elements belongs to $\mathcal{U}$;
\item $Q_k\notin\mathcal{W}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then every variety in $[\mathcal{U},\mathcal{W}]$ has infinite axiomatic rank.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{V}\in[\mathcal{U},\mathcal{W}]$ and let $k\geqslant 1$. Any assignment of at most $k$ variables into $Q_k$ has its image in a subsemiring belonging to $\mathcal{U}$, and hence to $\mathcal{V}$. Thus $Q_k$ satisfies every identity of $\mathcal{V}$ involving at most $k$ variables. Since $Q_k\notin\mathcal{W}$, it does not belong to $\mathcal{V}$. Those identities therefore do not form a basis for $\mathcal{V}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:characters}
Let $M$ be a finite $R$-module.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Every homomorphism from a submodule of $M$ to $R$ extends to a homomorphism $M\to R$.
\item Homomorphisms $M\to R$ separate the elements of $M$, and $|\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)|=|M|$.
\item Every submodule of $M$ isomorphic to $R^s$ is a direct summand of $M$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For (i), suppose that $\chi:N\to R$ is defined on a submodule $N$, and choose $x\in M\setminus N$. Let $\ell$ be the order of $x$ and $d$ the order of $x+N$ in $M/N$. Then $d\mid\ell\mid n$ and $dx\in N$. The element $a=\chi(dx)$ is annihilated by $\ell/d$, so in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ it is a multiple of $nd/\ell$ and, consequently, belongs to $dR$. Choose $b\in R$ with $db=a$. The rule
\[
 \chi'(y+kx)=\chi(y)+kb\qquad(y\in N,\ k\in\mathbb{Z})
\]
is well-defined and extends $\chi$ to $N+\langle x\rangle$. Iteration proves (i).

If $0\ne x\in M$ has order $d$, the homomorphism $\langle x\rangle\to R$ sending $x$ to $n/d$ is nonzero at $x$; apply (i). For the counting assertion, decompose $M$ into cyclic groups of orders dividing $n$ and use $|\operatorname{Hom}(C_d,C_n)|=d$.

Finally, if $F\leqslant M$ has basis $v_1,\ldots,v_s$ over $R$, extend its coordinate maps $F\to R$ to maps $\chi_i:M\to R$ using (i). The map
\[
 M\longrightarrow F,\qquad x\longmapsto\sum_{i=1}^{s}\chi_i(x)v_i
\]
is a retraction, proving (iii).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:nonzero}
Suppose $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_s\in R$ satisfy
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{s}\lambda_i=1
\]
and the coefficient vector is not a standard basis vector. Then there exist $y_0,\ldots,y_s\in H\setminus\{0\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonzero_relation}
 \sum_{i=0}^{s}\lambda_i y_i=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
A nonunit $a\in R$ annihilates some nonzero element of $H$: indeed, $H$ contains a cyclic subgroup of order $n$, and multiplication by $a$ on that subgroup has a nontrivial kernel. Also, if $a\ne 0$ in $R$, then $ah\ne 0$ for some $h\in H$, by the definition of the exponent.

For every integer $k\geqslant 2$, one can choose $k$ nonzero elements of $H$ with sum zero. For $k=2$ use $h,-h$. For $k=3$ choose nonzero $a,b$ with $b\ne-a$, and use $a,b,-a-b$; such a choice exists because $|H|\geqslant 3$. The general case follows by writing $k$ as a sum of twos and threes.

If none of the $\lambda_i$ is a unit, choose each $y_i\ne 0$ in the kernel of multiplication by $\lambda_i$. If at least two coefficients are units, choose nonzero values with sum zero for the products $\lambda_i y_i$ at the unit positions, and choose kernel elements at every other position.

It remains to consider exactly one unit coefficient, say $\lambda_j$. Some other coefficient $\lambda_k$ is nonzero; otherwise the normalization would make the coefficient vector a standard basis vector. Choose $y_k$ with $\lambda_k y_k\ne 0$, set $y_j=-\lambda_j^{-1}\lambda_k y_k$, and choose nonzero kernel elements at the remaining positions. These choices satisfy \eqref{eq:nonzero_relation}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A nonempty subset $C$ of an $R$-module $M$ is an \emph{$H$-kernel blocker} if
\[
 C\cap\ker f\ne\varnothing\qquad\text{for every }f\in\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,H).
\]
For a nonempty finite set $C\subseteq M$, define its \emph{difference submodule} by
\[
 L(C)=\langle c-c':c,c'\in C\rangle_R.
\]
For any $c_0\in C$, its affine hull is the coset $c_0+L(C)$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:defect}
If $C\subseteq M\setminus\{0\}$ is an $H$-kernel blocker, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:defect}
 |L(C)|<n^{|C|-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Write $C=\{c_0,\ldots,c_s\}$. The module $L=L(C)$ is generated by the $s$ differences $v_i=c_i-c_0$, so $|L|\leqslant n^s$. Suppose equality holds. Then the natural surjection $R^s\to L$ is an isomorphism, and the $v_i$ form an $R$-basis of $L$.

First suppose $c_0\notin L$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:characters}, there is a homomorphism $M/L\to R$ that is nonzero on $c_0+L$. Embed $R$ into $H$ as a cyclic subgroup of order $n$. The resulting map $M\to H$ has the same nonzero value on every $c_i$, contradicting the blocker property.

Suppose instead that $c_0\in L$, and write $c_0=\sum_{i=1}^{s}a_i v_i$. Put
\[
 \lambda_0=1+\sum_{i=1}^{s}a_i,\qquad \lambda_i=-a_i\quad(1\leqslant i\leqslant s).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:affinerel}
 \sum_{i=0}^{s}\lambda_i=1,\qquad \sum_{i=0}^{s}\lambda_i c_i=0.
\end{equation}
The vector $(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_s)$ cannot be a standard basis vector, since that would force one of the $c_i$ to be zero. Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero} supplies nonzero $y_i\in H$ satisfying the corresponding relation.

Define $f_0:L\to H$ on its basis by $f_0(v_i)=y_i-y_0$. Equation~\eqref{eq:affinerel} for the $y_i$ gives $f_0(c_0)=y_0$, and hence $f_0(c_i)=y_i$ for every $i$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:characters}(iii), $L$ is a direct summand of $M$, so $f_0$ extends to a homomorphism $M\to H$. This map is nonzero on all of $C$, again a contradiction. Therefore equality is impossible, proving \eqref{eq:defect}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:occurrence}
The set $B_\varepsilon$ is an $H$-kernel blocker in $W_\varepsilon$. If $0\in B_\varepsilon$, then $\mathbf{q}\preceq\mathbf{u}$ holds in $\mathcal{P}(M)$ for every $R$-module $M$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $f:W_\varepsilon\to H$ be an $R$-homomorphism. Since the inequality holds in $\mathcal{P}(H)$ and the sets $f(Y_i)$ are nonempty,
\[
 f(\alpha_\varepsilon)
 \in\mathbf{q}(f(Y_1),\ldots,f(Y_\ell))
 \subseteq\mathbf{u}(f(Y_1),\ldots,f(Y_\ell))
 =f\bigl(\mathbf{u}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_\ell)\bigr).
\]
Hence $f$ vanishes on a member of $B_\varepsilon$.

Suppose that $0\in B_\varepsilon$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_\ell$ be nonempty subsets of an $R$-module $M$, and choose $p\in\mathbf{q}(X_1,\ldots,X_\ell)$. Express $p$ by choosing an element of $X_i$ at each occurrence of $x_i$ in $\mathbf{q}$, and send $e_{i,j}$ to the corresponding element. If $t_i=0$, send the auxiliary vector $e_{i,1}$ to any element of $X_i$. The resulting homomorphism $\psi:W_\varepsilon\to M$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:occurrencemap}
 \psi(\alpha_\varepsilon)=p,\qquad \psi(Y_i)\subseteq X_i.
\end{equation}
Since $\alpha_\varepsilon\in\mathbf{u}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_\ell)$, it follows that
\[
 p\in\psi\bigl(\mathbf{u}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_\ell)\bigr)
 =\mathbf{u}(\psi(Y_1),\ldots,\psi(Y_\ell))
 \subseteq\mathbf{u}(X_1,\ldots,X_\ell).
\]
This proves the inequality in $\mathcal{P}(M)$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:congruence}
The relation $\theta_{\mathcal{E}}$ is a semiring congruence. The quotient
\[
 Q_{\mathcal{E}}(V)=\mathcal{P}(V)/\theta_{\mathcal{E}}
\]
is a finite commutative ai-semiring.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The family $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$ is upward closed and invariant under translations. If $X\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$ and $Z\in\mathcal{P}(V)$, then $X\cup Z$ belongs to the family. Choosing $z\in Z$, we also have $X+z\subseteq X+_V Z$, so $X+_V Z$ belongs to the family. These facts prove compatibility with addition and multiplication. The quotient is finite and commutative because $V$ is finite and abelian.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:fragmentmodel}
For every finite $R$-module $V$, the semiring $Q_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$ satisfies every inequality in $\mathcal{E}$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Fix $\varepsilon=(\mathbf{q}\preceq\mathbf{u})\in\mathcal{E}$ and nonempty representatives $X_1,\ldots,X_\ell$ for an assignment into the quotient. If $\mathbf{q}(X)\subseteq\mathbf{u}(X)$, the inequality holds under this assignment.

Otherwise choose $p\in\mathbf{q}(X)\setminus\mathbf{u}(X)$ and construct $\psi$ as in~\eqref{eq:occurrencemap}, including the choices for auxiliary vectors. Then
\[
 \psi(\alpha_\varepsilon)=p,\qquad
 \psi\bigl(\mathbf{u}(Y)\bigr)\subseteq\mathbf{u}(X).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:occurrence} implies $0\notin B_\varepsilon$. Moreover, $0\notin\psi(B_\varepsilon)$: an equality $\psi(\alpha_\varepsilon-b)=0$ with $b\in\mathbf{u}(Y)$ would imply $p\in\mathbf{u}(X)$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:forcing}
 p+(-\psi)(B_\varepsilon)
 =p-\psi(B_\varepsilon)
 =\psi\bigl(\mathbf{u}(Y)\bigr)\subseteq\mathbf{u}(X)
\end{equation}
is a forbidden configuration. Both $\mathbf{u}(X)$ and $\mathbf{u}(X)\cup\mathbf{q}(X)$ belong to $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$ and therefore have the same quotient class. This proves the inequality.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:types}
For the fixed family $\mathcal{E}$, only finitely many affine types of sets $\phi(B_\varepsilon)$ with $0\notin\phi(B_\varepsilon)$ occur as the finite target module varies. Every representative $C$ satisfies
\[
 |L(C)|<n^{|C|-1}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
For a fixed $W_\varepsilon$, two maps with the same kernel induce an isomorphism between their images carrying one image of $B_\varepsilon$ onto the other. There are finitely many submodules of $W_\varepsilon$ and finitely many retained blockers, which proves finiteness of the types.

The set $\phi(B_\varepsilon)$ is an $H$-kernel blocker in $\phi(W_\varepsilon)$: compose any homomorphism from that image module to $H$ with $\phi$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:occurrence}. Proposition~\ref{prop:defect} gives the inequality. Both cardinalities are invariant under affine isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:sparse}
Let $n\geqslant 2$, let $R=\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be a finite family of nonempty configurations in finite $R$-modules, each satisfying
\[
 |L(C)|<n^{|C|-1}.
\]
Fix constants $\eta>0$, $b\geqslant 1$, and $a\geqslant 1$. For each positive integer $r$, let $\mathcal{T}_r$ be a nonempty family of at most $ab^r$ subsets of $R^r$, each of cardinality at least $\eta n^r$. Then, for all sufficiently large $r$, there exists
\[
 D\subseteq R^r\setminus\{0\},\qquad |D|\leqslant 2r^2,
\]
which meets every member of $\mathcal{T}_r$ and contains no affine copy of any member of $\mathcal{C}$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Write $N=n^r$ and select each nonzero point of $R^r$ independently with probability $p=r^2/N$, obtaining a random set $D_r$. For sufficiently large $r$, $p<1$. The probability of missing at least one member of $\mathcal{T}_r$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hittingprob}
 ab^r(1-p)^{\eta N-1}
 \leqslant ab^r\exp\bigl(-p(\eta N-1)\bigr)=o(1).
\end{equation}

Fix $C\in\mathcal{C}$, choose $c_0\in C$, and put $h=|C|$ and $L=L(C)$. An affine copy of $C$ in $R^r$ has the form
\[
 z+\iota(C-c_0),
\]
where $z\in R^r$ and $\iota:L\to R^r$ is an injective homomorphism. By Lemma~\ref{lem:characters}(ii), the number of such copies is at most
\[
 N|\operatorname{Hom}_R(L,R^r)|=N|L|^r.
\]
A copy containing zero is never contained in $D_r$; every other copy is contained in $D_r$ with probability $p^h$. Hence the expected number of copies is at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:copyprob}
 N|L|^r p^h
 =r^{2h}\left(\frac{|L|}{n^{h-1}}\right)^r=o(1).
\end{equation}
Summing over the fixed finite family and applying Markov's inequality shows that the probability of containing a forbidden copy is $o(1)$.

Finally, $\mathbb{E}|D_r|<r^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(|D_r|)\leqslant r^2$. Chebyshev's inequality therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb{P}(|D_r|>2r^2)\leqslant r^{-2}.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:hittingprob} and \eqref{eq:copyprob}, this shows that the probability of any failure tends to zero. The required set exists for every sufficiently large $r$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:fibres}
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $m\geqslant 2$ be divisible by $\operatorname{exp}(G)$. For $g_1,\ldots,g_r\in G$ and $g\in\langle g_1\rangle\cdots\langle g_r\rangle$, the number of tuples $(k_1,\ldots,k_r)\in\{1,\ldots,m\}^r$ satisfying
\[
 g_1^{k_1}\cdots g_r^{k_r}=g
\]
is at least
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fibredensity}
 m^{-(|G|-1)}m^r.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Choose each $k_i$ independently and uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Then $g_i^{k_i}$ is uniform on $K_i=\langle g_i\rangle$. Let $\mu_i$ be the distribution of the product of the first $i$ factors, and put
\[
 S_0=\{1_G\},\qquad S_i=K_1\cdots K_i.
\]
Each $S_i$ is the support of $\mu_i$, and $S_{i-1}\subseteq S_i$ because $1_G\in K_i$. Let $\delta_i$ be the smallest positive value of $\mu_i$, with $\delta_0=1$. Convolution gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:convolution}
 \mu_i(x)=\frac{1}{|K_i|}\sum_{h\in K_i}\mu_{i-1}(xh^{-1}).
\end{equation}
If $S_i=S_{i-1}$, then $S_{i-1}K_i=S_{i-1}$; for each $x\in S_i$, every summand in \eqref{eq:convolution} is at least $\delta_{i-1}$. Thus $\delta_i\geqslant\delta_{i-1}$. If the support grows strictly, at least one summand is positive, so
\[
 \delta_i\geqslant\delta_{i-1}/|K_i|\geqslant\delta_{i-1}/m.
\]
There are at most $|G|-1$ strict support increases. Consequently $\delta_r\geqslant m^{-(|G|-1)}$. Multiplying this probability bound by $m^r$ proves \eqref{eq:fibredensity}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:dense}
The sets $T_{G,\boldsymbol{g}}$ satisfy the hypotheses on $\mathcal{T}_r$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:sparse}, with constants independent of $r$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $M=\max_{G\in\mathcal{G}}|G|$ and $\eta=m^{-(M-1)}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:fibres}, at least $\eta m^r$ exponent tuples give the target product $g_1\cdots g_r$. The reduction map
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_r)\longmapsto(1-k_1,\ldots,1-k_r)\pmod n
\]
has fibres of size exactly $(m/n)^r$. Therefore
\[
 |T_{G,\boldsymbol{g}}|\geqslant\eta n^r.
\]
There are at most $tM^r$ sets in the family. Taking $k_i=1$ for every $i$ shows that each set contains zero.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:relative}
Let $H$ be a finite abelian group with $|H|\geqslant 3$, and let $\mathcal{G}=\{G_1,\ldots,G_t\}$ be a nonempty finite family of finite groups. For every finite set $\Sigma\subseteq\operatorname{Id}(\mathcal{P}(H))$, there exist a finite commutative ai-semiring $Q$ and an inequality $\varepsilon$ such that
\[
 Q\models\Sigma,\qquad Q\not\models\varepsilon,
 \qquad \mathcal{P}(G_j)^0\models\varepsilon\quad(1\leqslant j\leqslant t).
\]
The separating inequality can be chosen so that every word on both sides has the same content. Moreover, with $n=\operatorname{exp}(H)$, the semiring $Q$ may be taken to be a quotient of $\mathcal{P}((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^r)$ for some positive integer $r$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Put $n=\operatorname{exp}(H)$ and $R=\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:reduction} to $\Sigma$, obtaining a finite family $\mathcal{E}$ of word inequalities valid in $\mathcal{P}(H)$. Form its occurrence blockers and let $\mathcal{C}$ contain one representative of each affine type from Lemma~\ref{lem:types}. If no blocker is retained, take $\mathcal{C}=\varnothing$.

Choose $m$ as in \eqref{eq:commonexponent}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sparse} and Corollary~\ref{cor:dense}, for some sufficiently large $r$ there is a set
\[
 D\subseteq R^r\setminus\{0\},\qquad |D|\leqslant 2r^2,
\]
which contains no affine copy of a member of $\mathcal{C}$ and meets every set $T_{G,\boldsymbol{g}}$. In particular $D$ is nonempty.

For $a\in R$, define the one-variable polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{eq:liftpoly}
 \mathbf{p}_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{1\leqslant k\leqslant m\\ k\equiv 1-a\;(\mathrm{mod}\ n)}}x^k.
\end{equation}
There are exactly $m/n$ summands, each with a positive exponent. For $d=(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in D$, put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:separatorpoly}
 \mathbf{q}_r=x_1x_2\cdots x_r,\qquad
 \mathbf{u}_D=\sum_{d\in D}\mathbf{p}_{d_1}(x_1)\mathbf{p}_{d_2}(x_2)\cdots \mathbf{p}_{d_r}(x_r).
\end{equation}
The order of the factors is $1,2,\ldots,r$ in every summand. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:epsilon}
 \varepsilon:\qquad\mathbf{q}_r\preceq\mathbf{u}_D
\end{equation}
holds in $\mathcal{P}(G)^0$ for every $G\in\mathcal{G}$.

Indeed, let $X_1,\ldots,X_r\subseteq G$. If some $X_i$ is empty, then both terms in the inequality have empty value, since every expanded monomial contains every variable with positive exponent. Otherwise take an arbitrary
\[
 g=g_1\cdots g_r\in X_1X_2\cdots X_r,
 \qquad g_i\in X_i.
\]
Choose $d\in D\cap T_{G,\boldsymbol{g}}$ and exponent witnesses $k_i$ from \eqref{eq:targetset}. The word $x_1^{k_1}\cdots x_r^{k_r}$ occurs in the expansion of the $d$-summand of \eqref{eq:separatorpoly}, and
\[
 g=g_1^{k_1}\cdots g_r^{k_r}
   \in X_1^{k_1}\cdots X_r^{k_r}
   \subseteq\mathbf{u}_D(X_1,\ldots,X_r).
\]
This proves the claim.

Now set $V=R^r$ and $Q=Q_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:fragmentmodel} and \ref{lem:reduction}, $Q\models\Sigma$. Let $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ be the standard basis of $V$, and put $\beta=e_1+\cdots+e_r$. Evaluate the variables at the quotient classes of the singletons $\{e_i\}$. Before taking the quotient, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:evaluation}
 \mathbf{q}_r(\{e_1\},\ldots,\{e_r\})=\{\beta\},\qquad
 \mathbf{u}_D(\{e_1\},\ldots,\{e_r\})=K:=\beta-D.
\end{equation}
The second equality holds because all exponents in $\mathbf{p}_{d_i}$ have the same residue $1-d_i$ modulo $n$.

The set $K$ does not belong to $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$. Otherwise it would contain $a+\phi(B)$ for a retained blocker with $0\notin\phi(B)$. The affine bijection $v\mapsto\beta-v$ would then place
\[
 (\beta-a)+(-\phi)(B)
\]
inside $D$, contrary to the avoidance property and the definition of $\mathcal{C}$.

Also $\beta\notin K$ because $0\notin D$. The class of $K$ is a singleton congruence class, so $K$ and $K\cup\{\beta\}$ have distinct classes, whether or not the latter belongs to the collapsed family. Consequently,
\[
 [K]+[\{\beta\}]=[K\cup\{\beta\}]\ne[K].
\]
Thus $Q\not\models\varepsilon$, while \eqref{eq:epsilon} holds in every $\mathcal{P}(G_j)^0$. This proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:abeliansubgroup}
Every finite group of order at least three contains an abelian subgroup of order at least three.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
If an element has order greater than two, its cyclic subgroup suffices. Otherwise every element is its own inverse, and $xy=(xy)^{-1}=yx$ for all $x,y$. The group itself is then abelian.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:localwitness}
Let $H$ be a finite group with $|H|\geqslant 3$, and let $G_1,\ldots,G_t$ be finite groups. For every $k\geqslant 1$, there are a finite commutative ai-semiring $Q_k$ and an inequality $\sigma_k$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item every subsemiring of $Q_k$ generated by at most $k$ elements belongs to $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H))$;
\item $Q_k\not\models\sigma_k$;
\item $\mathcal{P}(H)^0,\mathcal{P}(G_1)^0,\ldots,\mathcal{P}(G_t)^0$ all satisfy $\sigma_k$;
\item every word on either side of $\sigma_k$ has the same content.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Choose an abelian subgroup $A\leqslant H$ with $|A|\geqslant 3$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:finitevariable}, there is a finite set $\Delta_k\subseteq\operatorname{Id}_k(\mathcal{P}(A))$ implying all of $\operatorname{Id}_k(\mathcal{P}(A))$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:relative} with lower group $A$, upper family $\{H,G_1,\ldots,G_t\}$, and finite fragment $\Delta_k$. This yields $Q_k$ and $\sigma_k$ satisfying (ii)--(iv), and $Q_k$ satisfies every identity in $\operatorname{Id}_k(\mathcal{P}(A))$.

Let $T$ be a subsemiring of $Q_k$ generated by $a_1,\ldots,a_k$, repeating generators if necessary. If two terms in $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ induce the same term function on $\mathcal{P}(A)$, their equality holds in $Q_k$ and hence under $x_i\mapsto a_i$. Therefore this assignment induces a surjective homomorphism from the relatively free $k$-generated semiring of $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(A))$ onto $T$. It follows that
\[
 T\in\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(A))\subseteq\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H)),
\]
which proves (i).
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{U}=\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H))$. For each $k\geqslant 1$, take $Q_k$ and $\sigma_k$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:localwitness}. The inequality $\sigma_k$ holds in every generating semiring of $\mathcal{W}$, so $Q_k\notin\mathcal{W}$. Every subsemiring of $Q_k$ generated by at most $k$ elements belongs to $\mathcal{U}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:local} now gives infinite axiomatic rank for each $\mathcal{V}$ in~\eqref{eq:maininterval}. Every finite identity basis has a finite bound on its number of variables, so each such $\mathcal{V}$ is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Take $H=G$ and $t=1$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:interval}. Since $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is a subsemiring of $\mathcal{P}(G)^0$, this proves Corollary~\ref{cor:zerointerval} and the nonfinite-basis assertion of Corollary~\ref{thm:classification}.

For $|G|=1$, the semiring $\mathcal{P}(G)^0$ is the two-element distributive lattice. Relative to the ai-semiring axioms, it has the finite basis
\[
 x^2\approx x,\qquad xy\approx yx,\qquad xy\preceq x.
\]
For $|G|=2$, we have $G\cong C_2$, and a basis for $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(C_2)^0)$ relative to the ai-semiring axioms is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C2basis}
 x^3\approx x,\qquad xy\approx yx
\end{equation}
by Ren and Zhao~\cite[Lemma~3.7]{rz}. Since the ai-semiring axioms form a finite set, both semirings are finitely based.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:finitejoins}
For finite groups $G_1,\ldots,G_t$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(G_1)^0,\ldots,\mathcal{P}(G_t)^0)$ is finitely based;
\item $\prod_{j=1}^{t}\mathcal{P}(G_j)^0$ is finitely based;
\item $|G_j|\leqslant 2$ for every $j$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
A finite direct product generates the join of the varieties generated by its factors, since each projection is onto and the product belongs to the join. This proves the equivalence of (i) and (ii). If $|G_j|\geqslant 3$ for some $j$, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:interval} with $H=G_j$. Otherwise the join is either $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(C_1)^0)$ or $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(C_2)^0)$, because $\mathcal{P}(C_1)^0$ embeds into $\mathcal{P}(C_2)^0$. Both are finitely based.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:mixed}
Let $G_1,\ldots,G_t$ be finite groups, and choose
\[
 S_j\in\{\mathcal{P}(G_j),\mathcal{P}(G_j)^0\}\qquad(1\leqslant j\leqslant t).
\]
If $|G_i|\geqslant 3$ for some $i$, then every variety in
\[
 [\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(G_i)),\mathsf{V}(S_1,\ldots,S_t)]
\]
has infinite axiomatic rank and is nonfinitely based. In particular, $\prod_{j=1}^{t}S_j$ is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The lower endpoint is contained in the upper endpoint because $\mathcal{P}(G_i)$ embeds into $S_i$. Each $S_j$ embeds into $\mathcal{P}(G_j)^0$, so the upper endpoint is contained in $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(G_1)^0,\ldots,\mathcal{P}(G_t)^0)$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:interval} and use the equality between the variety of a finite direct product and the join of the varieties of its factors.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:zerooperator}
Zero adjunction defines an extensive, monotone, idempotent operation on the lattice of ai-semiring varieties. For every nonempty family $\{S_i:i\in I\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zerogenerators}
 \bigl(\mathsf{V}\{S_i:i\in I\}\bigr)^0
 =\mathsf{V}\{S_i^0:i\in I\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Extensivity follows from the embedding $S\hookrightarrow S^0$, and monotonicity follows from the definition.

To prove~\eqref{eq:zerogenerators}, set $\mathcal{U}=\mathsf{V}\{S_i:i\in I\}$. Consider an inequality $\mathbf{q}\preceq\mathbf{u}$ with a word on the left that holds in every $S_i^0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:zeroidentity}, the term $D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})$ is nonempty and
\[
 S_i\models\mathbf{q}\preceq D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})\qquad(i\in I).
\]
The latter inequality therefore holds in every $S\in\mathcal{U}$, so $S^0\models\mathbf{q}\preceq\mathbf{u}$ for every such $S$. Lemma~\ref{lem:reduction} gives the assertion for arbitrary identities. The reverse containment follows because $S_i\in\mathcal{U}$.

Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:zeroidentity} and
\[
 D_{\mathbf{q}}\bigl(D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})\bigr)=D_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{u})
\]
show that $S^0$ and $(S^0)^0$ satisfy the same identities. Applying~\eqref{eq:zerogenerators} to the family of zero extensions of members of $\mathcal{U}$ yields $(\mathcal{U}^0)^0=\mathcal{U}^0$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:generalzero}
Let $G_1,\ldots,G_t$ be finite groups and put
\[
 \mathcal{W}=\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(G_1)^0,\ldots,\mathcal{P}(G_t)^0).
\]
Let $H$ be a finite group with $|H|\geqslant 3$, and suppose that
\[
 \mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H))\subseteq\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{W}.
\]
Then $\mathcal{U}^0\subseteq\mathcal{W}$, and every variety in $[\mathcal{U},\mathcal{U}^0]$ has infinite axiomatic rank and is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:zerooperator}, the variety $\mathcal{W}$ is fixed by zero adjunction. Monotonicity gives $\mathcal{U}^0\subseteq\mathcal{W}^0=\mathcal{W}$. Every variety in $[\mathcal{U},\mathcal{U}^0]$ therefore lies in the interval covered by Theorem~\ref{thm:interval}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:envelope}
For the choices in~\eqref{eq:equationalupper}, the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H)^0,\mathcal{P}(G_1)^0,\ldots,\mathcal{P}(G_t)^0)\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}$;
\item $\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}^0=\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}$;
\item every variety in $[\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H)),\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}]$ has infinite axiomatic rank and is nonfinitely based.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Part (i) follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:localwitness}(iii). For (ii), write $\sigma_k$ as $\mathbf{q}_k\preceq\mathbf{u}_k$. Every word in $\mathbf{u}_k$ has content $c(\mathbf{q}_k)$, so $D_{\mathbf{q}_k}(\mathbf{u}_k)=\mathbf{u}_k$. Lemma~\ref{lem:zeroidentity} shows that $S\models\sigma_k$ implies $S^0\models\sigma_k$. Thus $\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}^0\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}$, and extensivity gives equality.

For (iii), every subsemiring of $Q_k$ generated by at most $k$ elements belongs to $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H))$, whereas $Q_k\notin\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}$ because it fails $\sigma_k$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:local}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:envelopezero}
If $\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{P}(H))\subseteq\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}$, then every variety in $[\mathcal{U},\mathcal{U}^0]$ has infinite axiomatic rank and is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Monotonicity and Theorem~\ref{thm:envelope}(ii) give $\mathcal{U}^0\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{H,\mathcal{G}}$. The assertion follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:envelope}(iii).
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:infinite}
The semiring $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z})^0$ generates $\mathsf{CAI}$. If $\{m_j:j\in J\}$ is an unbounded set of positive integers, then
\[
 \mathsf{V}\{\mathcal{P}(C_{m_j})^0:j\in J\}=\mathsf{CAI}.
\]
In particular, both varieties are finitely based.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The displayed semirings are commutative. Suppose two terms in $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ have different distributive normal forms as finite sets of commutative monomials. Choose an integer $B\geqslant 2$ larger than every exponent occurring in either normal form, and assign
\[
 x_i\longmapsto\{B^{i-1}\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}.
\]
A monomial with exponent vector $(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ evaluates to $\{\sum_i a_iB^{i-1}\}$. Distinct exponent vectors give distinct values by uniqueness of base-$B$ expansion. Thus the two terms have different values in $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z})^0$.

For the cyclic family, choose $m_j$ larger than all the integer monomial values just obtained. Reduction modulo $m_j$ keeps these values distinct and separates the same two terms in $\mathcal{P}(C_{m_j})^0$. Hence in each case the common identities are precisely those of commutative ai-semirings, which have a finite basis.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:constants}
If $G$ is a finite group with $|G|\geqslant 3$, then $\mathcal{P}(G)^0_{\mathscr C}$ is nonfinitely based for every $\mathscr C\subseteq\{0,1\}$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Choose an abelian subgroup $H\leqslant G$ of order at least three, and let $\Sigma$ be a finite set of identities of $\mathcal{P}(G)^0_{\mathscr C}$. They also hold in $\mathcal{P}(H)^0_{\mathscr C}$. Normalize the terms by distributivity and the laws of the named constants. A normalized term is either $0$, when this symbol is present, or a nonempty sum of words; the empty word is allowed when $1$ is named. A valid identity cannot equate $0$ with a nonempty polynomial, as is seen by assigning $\{1_H\}$ to every variable.

Reduce identities between nonempty polynomials to word inequalities as in Lemma~\ref{lem:reduction}. In each inequality, assign the empty set to variables outside the content of its lower word. This gives a finite family $\mathcal{E}$ of valid inequalities whose upper words use only variables from the lower word. The family $\mathcal{E}$, together with the normalization laws, implies $\Sigma$. If the lower word is empty, the restricted upper term contains an empty word and the inequality is immediate; discard it.

For the remaining inequalities use the occurrence construction of Section~\ref{sec:quotients}. An empty upper word contributes the singleton $\{0\}$ in the additive module, which is preserved by all module homomorphisms. Thus the blocker property, the cardinality estimate, and the quotient argument give a finite quotient $Q_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$ satisfying $\mathcal{E}$ on nonempty subset representatives. Its multiplicative identity is the class of $\{0\}$.

Adjoin a new zero to $Q_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$ and interpret the chosen constants by this zero and the class of $\{0\}$. Each restricted inequality remains valid: an assignment of the new zero to a variable of the lower word makes that word zero; all other assignments are covered by the quotient argument. Consequently the expanded semiring $Q_{\mathcal{E}}(V)^0$ satisfies $\Sigma$.

Choose the dimension of $V$ and the separating inequality as in Theorem~\ref{thm:relative}, with upper family $\{G\}$. This inequality holds in $\mathcal{P}(G)^0_{\mathscr C}$ and fails in $Q_{\mathcal{E}}(V)$ under singleton assignments. The same failure holds in its zero extension. Thus every finite fragment $\Sigma$ has a model failing another identity of $\mathcal{P}(G)^0_{\mathscr C}$, proving the assertion.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
